name: Tarukavaneswarar (Paraithurainathar) Temple, Tirupparaithurai
deity: Shiva as Tarukavaneswarar (Paraithurainathar), with the goddess Pasumpon Mayilambikai (Hemavarnambikai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine on the south bank of the Kaveri, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with Chola-era inscriptions and later additions
dynasty: Chola-era patrons and later Tamil dynasties
summary: Tarukavaneswarar is the Lord of Tirupparaithurai, the Tevaram shrine among the parai trees on the Kaveri's bank, where tradition places Shiva's coming as the wandering mendicant Bhikshatana to the proud sages of the Taruka forest.

sections.history: Tirupparaithurai stands on the southern bank of the Kaveri in the Tiruchirappalli country, where the river, honoured here as the Akanda Kaveri, the unbroken Kaveri, runs broad and unhurried a short way before it parts into the Kaveri and the Kollidam. The place takes its name from the parai trees that once crowded this stretch of the bank, and the Tevaram hymns call it Tirupparaithurai, the sacred landing-place of the parai. The saints Sambandar and Appar sang here, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, and the later poet Arunagirinathar is also said to have praised it. Inscriptions of the Chola age survive in the temple, and the stone shrine seen today grew from the patronage of the Chola kings and the dynasties after them, who raised a long chain of Shiva temples along the banks of the Kaveri.
sections.architecture: Tirupparaithurai is a quiet riverside temple of the Dravidian tradition, loved for its sanctity rather than for great height. The sanctum holds Shiva as a linga, worshipped as Tarukavaneswarar and as Paraithurainathar, the Lord of the parai grove. The goddess Pasumpon Mayilambikai, known also as Hemavarnambikai, the golden-hued mother, is honoured in a shrine of her own. Around the main sanctum are shrines to Vinayaka, Murugan, Mahalakshmi and Durga. In the outer corridor behind the sanctum grows the sacred parai tree, the living reminder of the grove from which the place takes its name.
sections.legends: The temple keeps the story of the Tarukavana, the forest of parai trees, where a company of sages lived who held that ritual alone, rightly performed, could command all things, and who had grown proud of it, forgetting the Lord for whom the rites were made. To humble them, Shiva came into the forest as Bhikshatana, the wandering mendicant, radiant and unclothed, with Vishnu beside him in the form of the enchanting Mohini. The sages and their wives were drawn to the wanderers, and in anger the sages kindled sacrifices and sent a serpent, a tiger and an elephant against Shiva. He mastered each in turn, and the sages, seeing that no rite can bind the One for whom all rites exist, bowed before him. Tirupparaithurai is remembered as the place where this lesson was taught, and the parai tree behind the sanctum is held sacred to this day; devotees pour water at its foot, praying for relief from illness, especially of the skin.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed with devotion, as at every Shiva temple, and the temple keeps a round of yearly festivals through the months of the Tamil calendar. The Aadi Perukku river festival, kept by the people along the Kaveri in July and August, gives the riverside setting a special warmth. Confirm the dates of any particular festival locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar and the temple's own almanac.
sections.experience: Come to Tirupparaithurai for the calm of the river rather than for grandeur. Offer your prayers first to Tarukavaneswarar in the sanctum, then to the golden goddess Pasumpon Mayilambikai in her shrine, and pause at the smaller shrines of Vinayaka, Murugan, Mahalakshmi and Durga. Many devotees walk the outer corridor to the sacred parai tree and pour a little water at its foot, and the Kaveri itself, never far away, is part of the pilgrimage. The temple lies beside a busy highway, yet within its walls it keeps the stillness of an old sanctuary on the water.

visit.timings: Commonly reported as open from about 6:00 to 11:30 in the morning and again from about 4:30 to 8:30 in the evening, with a midday closure; sources differ, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirupparaithurai lies on the Tiruchirappalli–Karur main road, about 16 km from the Chatram bus stand in Tiruchirappalli, and a bus stop stands close to the temple. Tiruchirappalli Junction is the main railway hub, and the city's airport is the nearest for air travellers. The Tiruchirappalli–Palakkad rail line also passes through the village area (Elamanur station); confirm train halts before relying on it. There are few eateries along the way, so it is wise to eat in Tiruchirappalli beforehand.
